'''Cragside''' is a [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor Revival]] country house near the town of [[Rothbury]] in [[Northumberland]], England. Dating to the [[Victorian era]], it was the home of [[William Armstrong, 1st Baron Armstrong]], founder of the [[Armstrong Whitworth]] armaments firm. An industrial [[magnate]], scientist, philanthropist and inventor of the [[hydraulic crane]] and the [[Armstrong gun]], Armstrong also displayed his inventiveness in the domestic sphere, making Cragside the first house in the world to be lit using [[hydroelectricity|hydroelectric]] power. The estate was technologically advanced: the architect of the house, [[Richard Norman Shaw]], wrote that it was equipped with "wonderful hydraulic machines that do all sorts of things".{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=17}} In the grounds, Armstrong built dams and lakes to power a sawmill, a water-powered laundry, early versions of a dishwasher and a [[dumb waiter]], a hydraulic [[elevator|lift]] and a hydroelectric [[rotisserie]]. In 1887, Armstrong was raised to the [[Peerages in the United Kingdom|peerage]], the first engineer or scientist to be ennobled, and became Baron Armstrong of Cragside.

The original building consisted of a small shooting lodge which Armstrong built between 1862 and 1864. In 1869, he employed the architect Richard Norman Shaw to enlarge the site, and in two phases of work between 1869 and 1882, they transformed the house into a northern [[Neuschwanstein]]. The result was described by the architect and writer [[Harry Stuart Goodhart-Rendel]] as "one of the most dramatic compositions in all architecture".{{sfn|Ferriday|1963|p=70}} Armstrong filled the house with a significant art collection; he and his wife were patrons of many [[Victorian painting|19th-century British artists]]. Cragside became an integral part of Armstrong's commercial operations: honoured guests under Armstrong's roof, including the [[Qajar dynasty|Shah of Persia]], the [[Monarchy of Thailand|King of Siam]] and two future [[Prime Minister of Japan|Prime Ministers of Japan]], were also customers for his commercial undertakings.

Following Armstrong's death in 1900, his heirs struggled to maintain the house and estate. In 1910, the best of Armstrong's art collection was sold off, and by the 1970s, in an attempt to meet [[inheritance tax]], plans were submitted for large-scale residential development of the estate. In 1971 the [[National Trust]] asked the architectural historian [[Mark Girouard]] to compile a gazetteer of the most important Victorian houses in Britain which the Trust should seek to save should they ever be sold. Girouard placed Cragside at the top of the list; in 1977, the house was acquired by the Trust with the aid of a grant from the [[National Land Fund]]. A [[listed building|Grade I listed building]] since 1953, Cragside has been open to the public since 1979.

==History==
[[File:William George Armstrong.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|Armstrong in the 1870s]]

===William Armstrong===
{{main article|William Armstrong, Baron Armstrong of Cragside}}
William Armstrong was born on 26 November 1810 in [[Newcastle upon Tyne]], the son of a corn merchant.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=6}} Trained as a solicitor, he moved to London before he was twenty. Returning to Newcastle, in 1835 he met and married Margaret Ramshaw, the daughter of a builder.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=7}} A keen amateur scientist, Armstrong began to conduct experiments in both hydraulics and electricity. In 1847, he abandoned the law for manufacturing and established [[Armstrong Whitworth|W. G. Armstrong and Company]] at a site at [[Elswick, Tyne and Wear|Elswick]], outside Newcastle.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=63}} By the 1850s, with his design for the [[Armstrong Gun]], Armstrong laid the foundations for an armaments firm that would, before the end of the century, see [[Krupp]] as its only world rival.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=13}}{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=106}} He established himself as a figure of national standing: his work supplying artillery to the [[British Army]] was seen as an important response to the failures of Britain's forces during the [[Crimean War]].{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=106}} In 1859, he was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] and made Engineer of Rifled Ordnance, becoming the principal supplier of armaments to both the Army and the [[Royal Navy]].{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=150}}{{efn|Britain's military deficiencies had been exposed in the Crimean War. At the time, Britain, in common with other European powers, had a nationalised gun-making industry.{{sfn|Friedman|2011|p=17}} Armstrong's appointment as Engineer of Rifled Ordnance saw the almost complete transfer of responsibility for production to his private [[Elswick Ordnance Company]]{{sfn|Johnston|Buxton|2013|pp=57–58}} and the development of the first breech-loading gun.{{sfn|Friedman|2011|p=17}} Commercial rivalries and governmental in-fighting saw the cancellation of all of Armstrong's contracts in 1862, and in 1863 he resigned his post, merging the EOC with his other engineering concerns to form Sir W G Armstrong and Co.{{sfn|Johnston|Buxton|2013|pp=57–58}}}}

===Shooting box: 1862–1865===
Armstrong had spent much of his childhood at [[Rothbury]], escaping from industrial Newcastle for the benefit of his often poor health.{{sfn|Dougan|1991|p=119}} He returned to the area in 1862, not having taken a holiday for over fifteen years.{{sfn|Heald|2012|pp=164–165}} On a walk with friends, Armstrong was struck by the attractiveness of the site for a house. Returning to Newcastle, he bought a small parcel of land and decided to build a modest house on the side of a moorland crag. He intended a house of eight or ten rooms and a stable for a pair of horses.{{sfn|Heald|2012|pp=164–165}} The house was completed in the mid-1860s by an unknown architect:{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} a two-storey [[Sporting lodge#Shooting Boxes|shooting box]] of little architectural distinction, it was nevertheless constructed and furnished to a high standard.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=168}}

===Fairy palace: 1869–1900===
Armstrong's architect for Cragside's expansion was the Scot [[R. Norman Shaw]]. Shaw had begun his career in the office of [[William Burn]] and had later studied under [[Anthony Salvin]] and [[George Edmund Street]].{{sfn|Brodie|Felstead|Franklin|Pinfield|2001|p=591}} Salvin had taught him the mastery of internal planning which was essential for the design of the large and highly variegated houses which the Victorian wealthy craved. Salvin and Street had taught him to understand the [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]].{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=118}} At only 24, he won the [[RIBA]] Gold Medal and Travelling Studentship.{{sfn|Turnor|1950|p=97}} The connection between Armstrong and Shaw was made when Armstrong purchased a picture, ''Prince Hal taking the crown from his father's bedside'' by [[John Callcott Horsley]], which proved too large to fit into his town house in [[Jesmond]], Newcastle.{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=117}} Horsley was a friend of both, and recommended that Shaw design an extension to the banqueting hall Armstrong had previously built in the grounds.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|pp=307–308}} When this was completed in 1869, Shaw was asked for enlargements and improvements to the shooting lodge Armstrong had had built at Rothbury four years earlier. This was the genesis of the transformation of the house between 1869 and 1884.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=80}} Over the next thirty years, Cragside became the centre of Armstrong's world; reminiscing years later, in his old age, he remarked, "had there been no Cragside, I shouldn't be talking to you today{{snd}}for it has been my very life".{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=165}}

The architectural historian [[Andrew Saint]] records that Shaw sketched out the whole design for the "future fairy palace" in a single afternoon, while Armstrong and his guests were out on a shooting party.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=80}} After this rapid initial design, Shaw worked on building the house for over 20 years. The long building period, and Armstrong's piecemeal, and changeable, approach to the development of the house, and his desire to retain the original shooting lodge at its core,{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=310}} occasionally led to tensions between client and architect, and to a building that lacks an overall unity.{{sfn|Saint|1992|pp=18–19}} Armstrong changed the purpose of several rooms as his interests developed, and the German architectural historian [[Hermann Muthesius]], writing just after Armstrong's death in 1900, noted that "the house did not find the unqualified favour with Shaw's followers that his previous works had done, nor did it entirely satisfy (Shaw)".{{sfn|Muthesius|1979|p=24}} Nevertheless, Shaw's abilities, as an architect and as a manager of difficult clients, ensured that Cragside was composed "with memorable force".{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=118}}

[[File:Cragside house top floor corridor.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|The top-lit Gallery, formerly Armstrong's museum]]
As well as being Armstrong's home, Cragside acted as an enormous display case for his ever-expanding art collection. The best of his pictures were hung in the drawing room, but Shaw also converted the museum into a top-lit picture gallery.{{sfn|Muthesius|1979|p=90}} Pride of place was given to [[John Everett Millais]]'s ''[[Chill October]]'', bought by Armstrong at the [[Samuel Mendel]] sale at [[Christie's]] in 1875. Armstrong also bought Millais' ''Jephthah's Daughter'' at the Mendel sale. Both were sold in the 1910 sale; ''Chill October'' is now in the private collection of [[Andrew Lloyd Webber]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/the-northerner/2013/mar/15/newcastle-energy|title=Palace of a modern magician |last=Sykes|first=Alan| date=15 March 2013|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=9 September 2017}}</ref> and ''Jephthah's Daughter'' is held by the [[National Museum Cardiff]].{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=282}}{{efn|There are conflicting views as to the price Armstrong paid for the paintings. His 2012 biographer Henrietta Heald quotes Armstrong in a letter to his wife: "I have bought ''Chill October'' and ''Jephthah'' for 900 [[Guinea (coin)|guineas]] – a big price but much less than they were expected to bring". Hugh Dixon, in the 2007 guidebook to Cragside, records that Armstrong paid 3,800 guineas for ''Jephthah's Daughter'' alone, "one of (his) most expensive purchases".{{sfn|Dixon|2007|p=9}} The art historian [[Gerald Reitlinger]] gives the following prices in his definitive guide: ''Chill October'', £3,255 and ''Jephthah's Daughter'', £3,990 (that is, 3,100 guineas and 3,800 guineas respectively). Their relative values had changed substantially by 1910: ''Chill October'' realised £5,040 but ''Jephthah'' only £1,260 (4,800 and 1,200 guineas).{{sfn|Reitlinger|1961|pp=389–390}}}}

Cragside was an important setting for Armstrong's commercial activities. The architectural writer [[Simon Jenkins]] records: "Japanese, Persian, Siamese and German dignitaries paid court to the man who equipped their armies and built their navies".{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=564–565}} In his 2005 book ''Landmarks of Britain'', [[Clive Aslet]] notes visits with the same purpose from the [[List of heads of state of Afghanistan|Crown Prince of Afghanistan]] and the [[Qajar dynasty|Shah of Persia]].{{sfn|Aslet|2005|pp=385–386}} The Shah [[Naser al-Din Shah Qajar|Naser al-Din]] visited in July 1889, and the Afghan prince [[Nasrullah Khan (Afghanistan)|Nasrullah Khan]] in June 1895.  Armstrong's biographer Henrietta Heald mentions two future prime ministers of Japan, [[Katō Takaaki]] and [[Saitō Makoto]], among a steady stream of Japanese industrialists, naval officers, politicians and royalty who inscribed their names in the Cragside visitors' book.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=278}} The Chinese diplomat [[Li Hung Chang]] visited in August 1896.  King [[Chulalongkorn]] of Siam was staying in August 1897, when activity at the Elswick Works was disrupted by a bitter [[strike action|strike]] over pay and hours.{{sfn|Smith|2005|p=33}}

In August 1884 the [[Prince of Wales|Prince]] and [[Princess of Wales|Princess]] of Wales (the future [[Edward VII]] and [[Alexandra of Denmark|Queen Alexandra]]) made a three-day visit to Cragside; it was the peak of Armstrong's social career. The royal arrival at the house was illuminated by ten thousand lamps and a vast array of [[Paper lantern|Chinese lanterns]] hung in the trees on the estate; fireworks were launched from six balloons, and a great bonfire was lit on the [[Simonside Hills]].{{sfn|Smith|2005|p=35}} On the second day of their visit, the Prince and Princess travelled to Newcastle, to formally open the grounds of Armstrong's old house, Jesmond Dean, which he had by then donated to the city as a public park. It is still a public park today, a ravine known as [[Jesmond Dene]].{{sfn|Smith|2005|p=37}} Three years later, at the [[Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria]], Armstrong was ennobled as Baron Armstrong of Cragside, and became the first engineer and the first scientist to be granted a peerage.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=294}}{{efn|Others have claimed the honour of the first scientific peerage for the physicist [[Lord Kelvin]] whose barony, awarded in 1892, was granted entirely in recognition of his scientific achievements.{{sfn|Smith|Norton Wise|1989|p=801}}{{sfn|Schobert|2014|p=154}}}} Among many other celebrations, he was awarded the freedom of the City of Newcastle. In his vote of thanks, the mayor noted that one in four of the entire population of the city was employed directly by Armstrong, or by companies over which he presided.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=296}}

===Armstrong's heirs: 1900–present===
Armstrong died at Cragside on 27 December 1900, aged 90, and was buried beside his wife in the churchyard at Rothbury.{{sfn|Smith|2005|p=44}} His gravestone carries an epitaph: ''His scientific attainments gained him a world wide celebrity and his great philanthropy the gratitude of the poor''.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1371120 |desc=Monument to First Lord Armstrong, Rothbury |date=25 August 1987 |access-date=14 September 2017}}</ref> Cragside, and Armstrong's fortune, were inherited by his great-nephew, [[William Watson-Armstrong, 1st Baron Armstrong|William Watson-Armstrong]].{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=121}} Watson-Armstrong lacked Armstrong's commercial acumen and a series of poor financial investments led to the sale of much of the great art collection in 1910.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=314}} In 1972, the death of Watson-Armstrong's heir, William John Montagu Watson-Armstrong, saw the house and estate threatened by large-scale residential development, intended to raise the money to pay a large [[inheritance tax]] bill.{{sfn|Binney|2007|p=389}} In 1971, when advising the National Trust on the most important Victorian houses to be preserved for the nation in the event of their sale, [[Mark Girouard]] had identified Cragside as the top priority.<ref name="buildingconservation2006">{{cite web|url=https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/cragside/cragside.htm |title=Cragside: Rewiring a Temple to High Victorian Technology|last1=Schmitz|first1=Sarah| last2=Rawson|first2=Caroline| date=2006|publisher=The Building Conservation Directory|access-date=9 September 2017}}</ref> A major campaign saw the house and grounds acquired by the Trust in 1977,{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=121}} with the aid of a grant from the [[National Land Fund]].{{sfn|Binney|2007|p=389}}

In 2007, Cragside reopened after undergoing an 18-month refurbishment programme<ref name="Restored: the world's first hydroelectric house">{{cite news|url= https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2007/apr/01/energy.theobserversuknewspages |title=Restored: the world's first hydroelectric house|access-date=17 July 2010 |newspaper=The Guardian|last = Thorpe|first=Vanessa | location=London | date=31 March 2007}}</ref> that included rewiring the whole house.<ref name="buildingconservation2006"/> It has become one of the most-visited sites in [[North East England]], with some 255,005 visitors in 2019.<ref name="ALVA 2019 visitor numbers">{{cite web |title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |access-date=4 November 2020}}</ref> The Trust continues restoration work, allowing more of the house to be displayed: Armstrong's electrical room, in which he conducted experiments on electrical charges towards the end of his life, was re-opened in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/news/north-east-news/see-inside-cragside-room-indulged-11693606 |title=The Cragside room which indulged Lord Armstrong's lifelong fascination with electricity |last=Henderson|first=Tony| date=2 August 2016|publisher=Chronicle Live |access-date=9 September 2017}}</ref> The experiments had led to the publication in 1897 of Armstrong's last work, ''Electrical Movement in Air and Water'', illustrated with remarkable early photographs by his friend John Worsnop.{{sfn|Smith|2005|p=42}}

The Trust continues the reconstruction of the wider estate, with plans to redevelop Armstrong's glasshouses, including the palm house, the ferneries and the orchid house.{{sfn|Dixon|2007|p=48}}

==Architecture and description==
[[File:Cragside House - geograph.org.uk - 5431615.jpg|thumb|The entrance front{{snd}} Shaw's "Wagnerian"{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} overture]]
Cragside is an example of Shaw's [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor revival]] style;{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} the [[Pevsner Architectural Guides|Pevsner Architectural Guide]] for Northumberland called it "the most dramatic [[Victorian era|Victorian]] mansion in the [[Northern England|North of England]]".{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} The entrance front was described by [[Harry Stuart Goodhart-Rendel]] as "one of the most dramatic compositions in all architecture",{{sfn|Ferriday|1963|p=70}} and the architectural historian [[James Stevens Curl]] regarded the house as "an extraordinarily accomplished [[Picturesque]] composition".{{sfn|Curl|1990|p=119}} Criticism focuses on the building's lack of overall coherence; in ''The National Trust Book of the English House,'' Aslet and Powers describe the house as "large and meandering",{{sfn|Aslet|Powers|1985|p=164}} and the architectural critics Dixon and Muthesius write that "the plan rambles along the hillside".{{sfn|Dixon|Muthesius|1993|p=54}} Saint is even more dismissive: for him, "the plan of Cragside is little better than a straggle".{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=82}} The [[Timber framing|half-timbering]] above the entrance has also been criticised as unfaithful to the [[vernacular architecture|vernacular]] tradition of the North-East.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} Shaw would have been unconcerned; desiring it for "romantic effect, he reached out for it like an artist reaching out for a tube of colour".{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=312}}

The architectural historian [[J. Mordaunt Crook]] considers Cragside to be one of the very few country houses built by the Victorian commercial [[plutocracy]] that was truly "[[avant-garde]] or trend-setting".{{sfn|Crook|1999|pp=70–71}} In his study, ''The Rise of the Nouveaux Riches'', Crook contends that many new-monied owners were too domineering, and generally chose second-rate architects, as these tended to be more "pliant", allowing the clients to get their own way, rather than those of the first rank such as Shaw.{{sfn|Crook|1999|pp=70–71}} The [[Rhineland|Rhenish]] flavour of the house makes a notable contrast with a country house that was almost contemporaneous with Cragside: the [[Villa Hügel]] constructed by Armstrong's greatest rival, [[Alfred Krupp]].{{sfn|Dougan|1991|p=118}} While Armstrong's Northumbrian fastness drew on [[Germanic peoples|Teutonic]] inspirations, his German competitor designed and built a house that was an exercise in [[neoclassical architecture|neoclassicism]].{{sfn|van Marle|Stewart|Walker|Williams|2015|p=667}}

The location for the house was described by Mark Girouard as "a lunatic site".{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=166}} Pevsner and Richmond call both the setting and the house Wagnerian.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} The ledge on which it stands is narrow, and space for the repeated expansions could only be found by dynamiting the rock face behind, or by building upwards. Such challenges only drove Armstrong on, and overcoming the technical barriers to construction gave him great pleasure.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=306}} His task was made easier by the use of the workforce and the technology of the Elswick Works.{{sfn|Heald|2012|pp=166–167}} The architectural historian Jill Franklin notes that the vertiginous fall of the site is so steep that the drawing room, on a level with the first-floor landing at the front of the house, meets the rock face at the back.{{sfn|Franklin|1981|p=211}}

Jenkins describes the plan of the house as "simpler than the exterior suggests".{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=564–565}} The majority of the reception rooms are located on the ground floor, as are the accompanying service rooms.{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=564–565}} The exception is the large extension Shaw added to the south-east from 1882.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=308}} This includes the drawing room, completed for the visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales, in August 1884.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=314}}

The house has been a [[listed building|Grade I listed building]] since 21 October 1953,<ref name="historicengland1"/> the listing citing ''inter alia'' its "largely complete Victorian interior".<ref name="historicengland1">{{NHLE|num=1042076 |desc=Cragside, Cartington |date=21 October 1953 |access-date=8 September 2017}}</ref>  The architectural correspondent of ''[[The Times]]'', [[Marcus Binney]], who was closely involved in the campaign to bring Cragside to the National Trust, noted the historic importance of this "virtually untouched interior",{{sfn|Binney|2007|pp=388–389}} with its collections of furnishings, furniture (much designed especially for Cragside), and fine and decorative arts, with work by many notable designers of the period, including [[William Morris]], [[Dante Gabriel Rossetti]], [[Philip Webb]] and [[Edward Burne-Jones]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/place/cragside |title=Cragside |publisher=National Trust Collections |access-date=14 September 2017}}</ref> Pevsner notes that the art collection demonstrated "what was permissible to the Victorian nobleman in the way of [[erotica]]".{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=246}}

===Kitchen, service rooms and Turkish bath===
[[File:Cragside Victorian Turkish baths Plunge.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|The plunge pool in the Victorian Turkish bath lined with [[Delftware]] tiles]]
The kitchen is large by Victorian standards and forms a considerable apartment with the butler's pantry.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} It displays Armstrong's "technical ingenuity" to the full, having a [[dumb waiter]] and a [[Rotisserie|spit]] both run on hydraulic power.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} An electric gong announced mealtimes.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2016|p=148}} For the visit of Edward and Alexandra, Armstrong brought in the Royal caterers, [[Gunter's Tea Shop|Gunters]], who used the kitchen to prepare an eight-course menu which included oysters, [[turtle soup]], stuffed [[turbot]], venison, grouse, peaches in [[maraschino]] jelly and [[brown bread ice cream]].{{sfn|Dixon|2007|pp=10–11}} Off the kitchen, under the library, is a [[Victorian Turkish baths|Victorian Turkish bath]],{{sfn|Shifrin|2015|pp=243-245}} an unusual item in a Victorian private house.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=244}} The writer Michael Hall suggests that the bath, with its plunge pool, was intended as much to demonstrate Armstrong's copious water supply as for actual use.{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=118}} As was often the case, Armstrong also found practical application for his pleasures: steam generated while warming dry air for the Turkish bath supported the provision of heating for the house.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=174}}

===Library and dining room===
[[File:Cragside library.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|The library{{snd}}"Shaw's greatest domestic interior"{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=84}}]]
Girouard describes the library as "one of the most sympathetic Victorian rooms in England".{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=312}} It belongs to the first phase of Shaw's construction work and was completed in 1872. It has a large [[bay window]] which gives views out over the bridge and the glen.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=52}} The room is half-panelled in oak and the fireplace includes fragments of Egyptian [[onyx]], collected during Armstrong's visit to the country in 1872.{{sfn|Saint|1992|pp=53–54}} The library originally contained some of Armstrong's best pictures, although most were rehung in the gallery or drawing room, following Shaw's later building campaign of the 1880s, and then sold in 1910, ten years after Armstrong's death.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=54}} The highlight was [[Albert Joseph Moore]]'s ''Follow My Leader'', dating from 1872.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=314}} Andrew Saint considers the room "Shaw's greatest domestic interior".{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=84}} The dining room off the library contains a "Gothic" fireplace with an [[inglenook]].{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=565}}{{efn|Shaw made the construction of inglenooks something of a speciality. He built his first at [[Cranbrook, Kent|Cranbrook]] for John Calcott Horsley, who later introduced Shaw to Armstrong.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=45}} As well as those at Cragside, two notable examples were created for the now-demolished [[Dawpool (house)|Dawpool Hall]] on the Wirral.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=290}} One of these now forms the porch of ''The Pantheon'' at [[Portmeirion]]<ref>{{Coflein|num=407058|desc=The Pantheon, Portmeirion|access-date=18 September 2018}}</ref> and the other went unsold on [[eBay]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/the-northerner/2012/jan/19/dawpool-ismay-titanic-wahite-star-line-victorian-society|title=Titanic owner's massive white elephant lumbers on to eBay|first=Martin|last=Wainwright|date=19 January 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=18 September 2018}}</ref> Shaw's biographer, Andrew Saint writes, "inglenooks are the decorative pièce de résistance of the Shaw [[English country house|country house]]".{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=137}}}}

A portrait of Armstrong by [[Henry Hetherington Emmerson]] shows him sitting in the inglenook with his dogs,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/1230258 |title=Sir William George Armstrong, 1st Baron Armstrong of Cragside (1810–1900), in the Inglenook at Cragside 1230258 |publisher=National Trust Collections |access-date=14 September 2017}}</ref> under a carved inscription on the mantlepiece reading ''East or West, [[wikt:hame#Scots|Hame's]] Best''.{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=565}} The stained glass in the windows of the inglenook is by William Morris, and other glass from [[Morris & Co.]], to designs by Rossetti, Burne-Jones, Webb and [[Ford Madox Brown]], was installed in the library, gallery and upper stairs.{{sfn|Dixon|2007|p=19}}

===Owl suite===
The Owl rooms were constructed in the first building campaign and formed a suite for important guests.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=106}}{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=63}} Their name derives from the carved owls that decorate the woodwork and the bed.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=63}} The room is panelled in [[Juglans nigra|American Black walnut]], the same wood from which the [[Four-poster bed|tester]] bed is carved.{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=565}} Saint notes that Shaw was "proud of the design", displaying a further "owl-bed" in an exhibition in 1877.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=194}} The Prince and Princess of Wales occupied the rooms during their stay at Cragside in 1884.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=63}} Other bedrooms, notably the Yellow and White rooms, were hung with wallpaper by William Morris, including early versions of his ''Fruit'' and ''Bird and Trellis'' designs. The wallpapers were reprinted using the original [[Woodblock printing|printing blocks]] and rehung in the National Trust's renovations.{{sfn|Dixon|2007|p=26}}

===Gallery===
The gallery originally formed Armstrong's museum room and was built by Shaw between 1872 and 1874.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|pp=245–246}} It led to the observatory in the Gilnockie Tower. Later, the room formed a processional route to the newly created drawing room, and was transformed into a gallery for pictures and sculpture.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=64}} Its lighting displayed further evidence of Armstrong's technical ingenuity. Provided with twelve overhead lamps, the lighting for the room could be supplemented by a further eight lamps, powered by electric current transferred from the lamps in the dining room when they were no longer required.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=288}} Lighting, and his means of providing it, mattered to Armstrong, on both technical and aesthetic levels; he wrote, "in the passageways and stairs the lamps are used without shades and present a most beautiful and star-like appearance."{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=288}}

===Drawing room===
{{See also|Arabella Goddard#Broadwood piano}}
[[File:Cragside, Northumberland - The Drawing Room.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|The drawing room and inglenook fireplace{{snd}}"sensational",{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=564–565}} "spectacular"{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=245}} or "sickening",{{sfn|Turnor|1950|p=101}} according to taste]]
The drawing room was constructed in the 1880s phase of building, when Armstrong had sold his Jesmond house and was residing solely at Cragside.{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=121}} Aslet suggests that the inspiration for the design was the [[great hall]] at [[Haddon Hall]], [[Derbyshire]],{{sfn|Aslet|2005|pp=385–386}} although Saint considers Shaw's [[Dawpool (house)|Dawpool Hall]], [[Cheshire]] as the more likely source.{{sfn|Saint|2010|p=290}}{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=66}} Pevsner and Richmond mention [[Hardwick Hall]] and [[Hatfield House]] as possible models for the "spectacular" overall design.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=245}} 

The room contains a colossal marble inglenook [[Fireplace mantel|chimneypiece]], reputed to weigh ten tons, and designed by Shaw's assistant, [[William Lethaby|W. R. Lethaby]].{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=66}} Muthesius describes the fireplace as a "splendid example ... with finely composed relief decoration".{{sfn|Muthesius|1979|p=185}} Jenkins considers it "surely the world's biggest inglenook" and describes the overall impact of the room as "sensational", noting the top-lit ceiling and the elaborate [[Jacobethan]] [[plasterwork]].{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|pp=564–565}} Others have been less complimentary; the writer Reginald Turnor, no admirer either of Shaw or of Victorian architecture and its architects more generally,{{sfn|Turnor|1950|p=6}} wrote of the room's "flamboyant and rather sickening detail".{{sfn|Turnor|1950|p=101}} By the time of its construction, Shaw, increasingly working for clients of great wealth, had moved on from his "Old English" style,{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=283}} and the room is designed and decorated in a grander and more opulent [[Renaissance Revival architecture|Renaissance]] taste.{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=121}}{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=107}} In 2025, a [[John Broadwood & Sons|Broadwood]] piano, originally owned by concert pianist [[Arabella Goddard]], was reinstalled into the drawing room. It made its first appearance in 1875, after Armstrong bought it in an auction for 250 [[guineas]], but then left the house some time after his death.<ref name="JournalOct25">

===Billiard room===
The billiard room extension of 1895 is by Frederick Waller.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1042076|desc=Cragside, Cartington |date= 1 January 1985 |access-date=16 December 2017}}</ref> It replaced a laboratory, in which Armstrong conducted experiments in electric currents.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=70}} The billiard table and furniture were supplied by [[Burroughes and Watts]].{{sfn|Dixon|2007|p=31}} The billiard room and adjacent gun room{{sfn|Franklin|1981|p=59}} formed a smoking suite, the previous absence of which is evidenced in a watercolour painted to commemorate the visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales. The Prince and Armstrong are shown smoking cigars on the terrace, as Victorian convention did not permit smoking in the principal reception rooms.{{sfn|Girouard|1979|p=317}}{{sfn|Dutton|1948|p=174}}{{efn|Attitudes towards smoking indoors changed significantly in the [[Victorian era|Victorian period]]. The architect [[Robert Kerr (architect)|Robert Kerr]], more famous for his textbook on the design of Victorian houses than for his buildings, wrote in 1864, "The pitiable resources to which some gentlemen are driven, even in their own houses, in order to be able to enjoy the pestiferous luxury of a cigar, have given rise to the occasional introduction of an apartment specially dedicated to the use of Tobacco."{{sfn|Kerr|2012|p=143}} The historian Jill Franklin noted that "smoking was still completely forbidden in some houses as late as the 1850s", and that only in "more tolerant houses could (gentlemen) use the servants' hall or the harness room of the stables".{{sfn|Franklin|1981|pp=56–57}}}}

==Technology==
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Cragside Archimedes' screw from bottom.jpg
| caption1          = Cragside's [[screw turbine]], installed in 2014
| image2            = Burnfoot Power House. Generator, turbine, etc, Cragside Estate, Rothbury, England.jpg

| total_width       = 400
}}
After his first visit in 1869, Shaw described the house in a letter to his wife, noting the "wonderful hydraulic machines that do all sorts of things you can imagine".{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=17}} By building dams, Armstrong created five new lakes on the estate, Debdon, Tumbleton, Blackburn, and the Upper and Lower lakes at Nelly's Moss.{{sfn|Saint|1992|pp=75–76}} In 1868, a [[hydraulic]] engine was installed. Inspired by a watermill on the [[River Dee, Cumbria|Dee]] in [[Dentdale]],{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=22}} in 1870 Armstrong installed a [[Siemens]] [[dynamo]] in what was the world's first [[hydroelectric power station]].{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=246}} The generators, which also provided power for the farm buildings on the estate, were constantly extended and improved to meet the increasing electrical demands in the house.  The 2006 regeneration project included extensive rewiring.<ref name="buildingconservation2006"/> A new [[screw turbine]], with a {{convert|17|m|ft|adj=on}}-long [[Archimedes' screw]], was installed in 2014; it can provide 12 kW, supplying around 10 per cent of the property's electricity consumption.{{efn|Armstrong also investigated the possibilities of applying technological innovations to agricultural activities; in the mid-1890s he constructed a hydraulic [[silage]] plant on the estate at [[Cragend Silo|Cragend Farm]]. It was not a success, due to the amount of manual labour required and the gases which the process produced.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1153196|desc=Hydraulic Silo building at Cragend Farm|grade=II*|access-date=25 April 2019}}</ref>}}<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/jul/31/national-trust-lights-up-historic-mansion-with-hydropower |title=National Trust lights up historic mansion with hydropower|last=Kirby|first=Alex| date=31 July 2014|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=9 September 2017}}</ref>

The electricity generated was used to power an [[arc lamp]] installed in the picture gallery in 1878. This was replaced in 1880 by [[Joseph Swan]]'s [[incandescent lamp]]s in what Swan considered "the first proper installation" of electric lighting.{{sfn|Aslet|2005|p=386}} Armstrong knew Swan well and had chaired the presentation of Swan's new lamps to the [[Literary and Philosophical Society of Newcastle upon Tyne]]. [[Historic England]] describes Cragside as the "first (house) in the world to be lit by electricity derived from water power".<ref name="historicengland1"/> The use of electricity to run the house's appliances and internal systems made Cragside a pioneer of [[home automation]]; one of the first private residences to have a dishwasher, a vacuum cleaner and a washing machine, the conservators Sarah Schmitz and Caroline Rawson suggest Cragside was "the place where modern living began".<ref name="buildingconservation2006"/> The spit in the kitchen was also powered by hydraulics.{{sfn|Aslet|2005|pp=385–386}} The conservatory contained a self-watering system for the pot plants, which turned on water-powered revolving stands.{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=118}} Telephony was introduced, both between the rooms in the house, and between the house and other buildings on the estate.{{sfn|Dougan|1991|p=122}} A plaque at [[Bamburgh Castle]], Armstrong's other residence on the Northumbrian coast, records that his development of these new automated technologies "emancipated ... much of the world from household drudgery".{{sfn|Cleary|2006|p=67}}

==Grounds and estate==
[[File:The Burn and footbridge, Cragside - geograph.org.uk - 1191568.jpg|thumb|upright|Armstrong's bridge over the Debdon Burn]]
Cragside is named after ''Cragend Hill'' above the house, and is surrounded by an extensive [[rock garden]], with a collection of [[rhododendron]]s, one of which is named after Lady Armstrong, who made a considerable contribution to the design and construction of the gardens,{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=299}} and  large plantings of mostly [[conifer]]ous trees.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/gardenstovisit/10021225/The-best-gardens-to-see-rhododendrons.html|title=The best gardens to see rhododendrons|newspaper=Daily Telegraph|access-date=27 August 2014}}</ref> Among these is the tallest [[Scots pine]] in Britain, at a height of {{convert|131|ft}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-tyne-27662841 |title=Cragside Scots pine tree is 'tallest of its kind' in UK – BBC News |author=BBC | publisher=BBC.co.uk |date=2 June 2014 |access-date=11 September 2017}}</ref> Over one hundred years after their planting, Jill Franklin wrote that, "the great, dark trees form a protective barrier to (Armstrong's) home".{{sfn|Franklin|1981|p=119}} Armstrong continued to buy land after the purchase of the original site and by the 1880s the gardens and grounds comprised some {{convert|1,700|acres}},{{sfn|Hall|2009|p=118}} with the wider estate, including Armstrong's agricultural holdings, extending to {{convert|15,000|acres}} according to Henrietta Heald's 2012 biography of Armstrong,{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=169}} and to over {{convert|16,000|acres}} according to the historian [[David Cannadine]].{{sfn|Cannadine|1992|p=202}} David Dougan records the traditional claim that Armstrong planted over seven million trees in the gardens and parkland.{{sfn|Dougan|1991|p=120}} The estate is a sanctuary for some of the last remaining [[red squirrel]] colonies in England.{{sfn|Binney|2007|p=389}}
The glen north-west of the house is spanned by an iron bridge, crossing the Debdon Burn, constructed to Armstrong's design<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.victorianweb.org/art/architecture/normanshaw/2.html |title=Cragside, by Richard Norman Shaw and other architects |last=Banerjee|first=Jacqueline|publisher=Victorianweb.org |date=2 March 2017 |access-date=11 September 2017}}</ref> at his [[Elswick Ordnance Company|Elswick Works]] in the 1870s.{{sfn|Pevsner|Richmond|2002|p=246}} It is a [[listed building|Grade II* listed structure]]<ref>{{NHLE|num=1042033 |desc=The Iron Bridge across the Debdon Burn, Rothbury|date=25 August 1987 |access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref> and was restored by the Trust, and reopened to the public in 2008–2009.{{sfn|Dixon|2007|pp=36–37}} The gardens themselves are listed Grade I,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1001046 |desc=Cragside Park and Gardens |date= 1 January 1985 |access-date=30 September 2017}}</ref> and some of the architectural and technological structures have their own historic listings.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1001046 |desc=Cragside, Brinkburn |date= 1 January 1985 |access-date=11 September 2017}}</ref> The Clock Tower, which regulated life on the estate,{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=75}} dates from the time of the construction of the shooting lodge, and might have been designed by the same architect; it is not by Shaw.{{sfn|Saint|1992|p=77}} It is possible that Armstrong himself designed the clock.<ref name="historicengland2"/> Like the bridge, the Clock Tower has a Grade II* listing.<ref name="historicengland2">{{NHLE|num=1354750 |desc=Clock Tower 110M north east of Cragside Park House|date= 25 August 1987 |access-date=14 September 2017}}</ref> The formal gardens, where Armstrong's great greenhouses stood and which were long separated from the main estate, have now been acquired by the Trust.{{sfn|Heald|2012|p=338}}

'''Lyveden New Bield''' (sometimes called New Build) is an unfinished [[Elizabethan]] summer house in the parish of [[Aldwincle]] in [[North Northamptonshire]], commissioned by Sir [[Thomas Tresham (died 1605)|Thomas Tresham]] and now owned by the [[National Trust]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=National Trust UK |title=Lyveden {{!}} Northamptonshire, Intriguing Elizabethan lodge and moated garden |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/leicestershire-northamptonshire/lyveden |access-date= |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> It is a [[Grade I listed building]], classing it as a 'building of exceptional interest.'<ref>{{cite web |title=LYVEDEN OLD BIELD AND ATTACHED OUTBUILDINGS |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1040347 |website=Historic England}}</ref>

==Construction==
It was constructed for Sir [[Thomas Tresham (died 1605)|Thomas Tresham]], the fervent [[Roman Catholic]] of [[Rushton Hall]], and is thought to have been designed by [[Robert Stickells]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=National Trust UK |title=History of Lyveden │ Northamptonshire |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/leicestershire-northamptonshire/lyveden/history-of-lyveden |access-date= |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> The exact date is unknown but can be estimated to circa 1604–05, the year of Tresham's death. The New Bield was on the estate of Tresham's second home, Lyveden Manor House, also known as Lyveden Old Bield.

== Design & Catholic Motifs ==
Just as at Tresham's smaller [[folly]], [[Rushton Triangular Lodge]], his principal estate, the New Bield has a religious design full of symbolism.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ross |first=David |title=Lyveden New Bield, History & Photos {{!}} Historic Northamptonshire Guide |url=https://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3662 |access-date= |website=Britain Express |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lyveden New Bield - Historic House in PETERBOROUGH, Peterborough - Visit Peterborough |url=https://www.visitpeterborough.com/things-to-do/lyveden-new-bield-p876601 |access-date= |website=www.visitpeterborough.com}}</ref> Designed on a plan reminiscent of a [[Greek cross]], the facades have a strict symmetry.<ref name=":1" /> The building has two floors above a raised [[basement]], with [[mullion]]ed and [[Transom (architectural)|transomed]] windows. Each floor had three rooms with a staircase in the south projection of the cross. 

The exterior of the building is decorated by [[friezes]] of a religious nature. The [[metope (architecture)|metopes]] contain the emblems and [[motif (art)|motifs]] found also at the triangular lodge, such as the "IHS" [[christogram]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Johnson |first=Lily |title=Lyveden New Bield is a historic lodge and gardens perfectly preserved in their original Elizabethan state. |url=https://www.historyhit.com/locations/lyveden-new-bield/ |access-date= |website=History Hit |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Purpose as a 'Secret House' ==
[[File:Ground Plan of Lyveden New Building (11095427725).jpg|thumb|Ground Plan of Lyveden New Building. ]]
The house was likely meant for occupation, as it has a [[great hall]] and [[parlour]] on the first floor, kitchen and buttery in the basement, and a bedroom on the upper floor. However, it was probably never intended for full-time occupation. Too close to the main house for use as a hunting lodge, it may have been intended for use as a "Secret House"—keeping a secret house was a custom of the 16th century.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Morcom |first=Jess |date=2022-01-23 |title=The Northants summer house standing unfinished for 400 years |url=https://www.northantslive.news/whats-on/whats-on-news/story-half-built-elizabethan-lodge-4291236 |access-date= |website=Northants Live |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=English Catholic History Association |date=2015 |title=Triangular Lodge & Lyveden New Bield |url=https://englishcatholichistoryassoc.files.wordpress.com/2015/08/triangular-lodge-and-lyveden-new-bield.pdf |journal=English Catholic History Association}}</ref> Often within a mile of the main house, the secret house was a place where the head of the household would retire for a few days with a minimum of servants, while the principal house was thoroughly cleaned and, bearing in mind the sanitation of the time, fumigated.<ref name=":2" /> Similar examples of "secret houses" exist at [[Leconfield]] and [[Warkworth, Northamptonshire|Warkworth]], where their use for this purpose has been well documented.

Lyveden New Bield was never completed. It remains as it was when the builders left following Sir Thomas Tresham's death. Today, it is in the care of the [[National Trust]].<ref name=":0" />

==Lyveden Old Bield==
Lyveden Manor House, now also known as Lyveden Old Bield, the once grand principal house of the [[Estate (house)|estate]], had belonged to the Tresham family from c.1450. Today, little remains and what does was probably built by Thomas Tresham's grandson Lewis. The gatehouse has been removed to [[Benefield#Fermyn Woods Hall|Fermyn Woods Hall]], and the staircase was transported to America, where it was incorporated in the [[Edsel and Eleanor Ford House]] near Detroit.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bell |first=Thomas |title=The Ruins Of Lyveden - With Historical Notices Of The Family Of Tresham And its Connexion With The Gunpowder Plot |publisher=Simpkin, Marshall & Co., Alfred King, Oundle |year=1872 |location=London, United Kingdom}}</ref> One wing remains with mullioned windows.

In 2013, the National Trust acquired Lyveden Manor House, it is open to the public, with the Trust's long-term aim to restore the historic gardens and open them to the public.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lyveden New Bield |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lyveden |website=National Trust}}</ref>

== Gardens & Orchard ==
[[File:Orchard, Lyveden New Bield - geograph.org.uk - 3703941.jpg|thumb|Orchard, Lyveden New Bield. ]]
Set on 60 acres Lyveden lies in the heart of the medieval [[Rockingham Forest|Royal Forest of Rockingham]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=An introduction to Lyveden New Bield {{!}} The National Trust |url=http://oldweb.lyveden.org.uk/ |access-date= |website=oldweb.lyveden.org.uk}}</ref> Tresham designed extensive gardens between the manor house and the New Bield, but for centuries little evidence of the gardens remained. However, in 2010, National Trust experts studying photographs taken by the [[Luftwaffe]] during the [[Second World War]] discovered the remains of an Elizabethan [[labyrinth]], garden and orchard in the grounds.<ref name="Tel2010">{{cite news |first=Louise |last=Gray |title=Photos taken by the enemy in Second World War shows lost Tudor garden |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/8112577/Photos-taken-by-the-enemy-in-Second-World-War-shows-lost-Tudor-garden.html |newspaper=The Daily Telegraph |date=6 November 2010 |accessdate=6 November 2010}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bradshaw |first=Mark |title=An Elizabethan Garden Un-covered {{!}} Lyveden New Bield 1995 – 2012 |url=https://www.lyveden.org.uk/ |access-date= |website=www.lyveden.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Kennedy |first=Maev |date=2010-11-06 |title=Luftwaffe spy photo reveals lost Tudor garden |url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2010/nov/06/luftwaffe-spy-tudor-garden-lyveden |access-date= |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The gardens were subsequently upgraded to a Grade I listing by [[English Heritage]].<ref name="Tel2010" />

The National Trust has reconstructed Tresham's orchard, which originally contained 300 fruit and nut trees, as well as restored the moat on three sides of the labyrinth.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trust |first=The Gardens |date= 23 January 2021|title=More on Lyveden |url=https://thegardenstrust.blog/2021/01/23/more-on-lyveden/ |access-date=2024-02-23 |website=The Gardens Trust |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Malpas |first=Laura |title=Lyveden, revisited and reconnected |url=https://www.northamptonshireheritageforum.co.uk/latest-news/lyveden-revisited-and-reconnected |access-date= |website=Northamptonshire Heritage Forum |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==The Tresham Family and The Gunpowder Plot==
[[File:Monteagle letter.jpeg|thumb|An anonymous letter, sent to [[William Parker, 4th Baron Monteagle]], was instrumental in revealing the plot's existence. Its author's identity has never been reliably established, although [[Francis Tresham]] has long been a suspect. ]]
Sir Thomas Tresham died in 1605 following decades of religious persecution, his once vast wealth having been severely depleted. His son [[Francis Tresham]] inherited the estate, but within the same year, along with his cousins [[Robert Catesby]] and [[Robert and Thomas Wintour]], he became involved in the [[Gunpowder Plot]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fraser |first=Antonia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ebWzoszYEZAC |title=The Gunpowder Plot: Terror & Faith in 1605 |date=1997 |publisher=Mandarin |isbn=978-0-7493-2357-8 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=UK Parliament |title=Francis Tresham |url=https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/evolutionofparliament/parliamentaryauthority/the-gunpowder-plot-of-1605/overview/people-behind-the-plot/francis-tresham-/ |website=parliament.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=UK Parliament |title=People behind the Gunpowder plot |url=https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/evolutionofparliament/parliamentaryauthority/the-gunpowder-plot-of-1605/overview/people-behind-the-plot/ |website=parliament.uk}}</ref> Thus, within a year the estate had a third owner, Francis's son [[Lewis Tresham]]. The estate was managed by Lewis's mother until her death in 1615.

After this, Lewis Tresham, a spendthrift, lost the remaining family wealth.<ref name=":1" /> The estate was eventually sold following the death of his son in 1643.

2445742.extract:
Allen Banks & Staward Gorge  is a 194-acre National Trust property in the English county of Northumberland.

The property has been designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest for its rich flora and fauna. There is a large suspension bridge which has been ruined by the flooding of January 2005.

'''Cherryburn''' is a [[cottage]] in [[Mickley, Northumberland|Mickley]], [[Northumberland]], England. It was the birthplace of [[Thomas Bewick]], an [[England|English]] [[wood engraving|wood engraver]] and [[ornithology|ornithologist]]. The cottage, its adjacent farmhouse and large grounds, have been managed by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 1991 when they took over responsibility for the site from the Bewick Birthplace Trust.<ref>{{cite book |last=Garnett |first=Oliver |title=Thomas Bewick and Cherryburn |date=2006 |publisher=[[The National Trust]] |location=Wiltshire |page=32}}</ref>  Cherryburn is open to the public.

== History ==

Thomas Bewick was born in the cottage in August 1753, he grew up there until the age of 14 when he moved to [[Newcastle upon Tyne]] to become a bound apprentice with the Beilby family.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Armstrong |first1=Jack |title=Bewick of Cherryburn |date=1970 |publisher=Frank Graham |location=Newcastle |pages=3, 5}}</ref>

The Cottage and the Farmhouse are now a museum to show what life was back when Thomas Bewick was alive. The Cottage has been furnished with items which would have been common at the time and the Farmhouse possesses a large collection of Bewick's publications, original engravings and printing equipment.<ref>{{cite web |title=Things to do at Cherryburn |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/north-east/cherryburn/things-to-do-at-cherryburn |publisher=[[The National Trust]] |access-date=21 November 2022 |quote=Built in the 19th century by the family of Bewick’s brother, the farmhouse is now a museum with an exhibition about Thomas’s life and an unrivalled collection of his original artworks.... Discover the process of how he created his artwork from wood block to final print with a demonstration in the print room....}}</ref>

25326219.title: Easton on the Hill
25326219.extract:
Easton on the Hill is a village and civil parish  at the extreme north eastern tip of North Northamptonshire, England. The village had a population at the 2011 census was 1,015. The village, sited on the A43 road, is compact in form, with the older part of the village located north of the High Street. The parish extends from the River Welland in the north to the western end of RAF Wittering. The village is also on the shortest boundary in England with it being in the northernmost part of Northamptonshire between Stamford and Collyweston.
The villages name means 'east farm/settlement' on the hill.
All Saints Church dates from the twelfth century and has been enlarged and altered over the centuries. The church is a Grade I listed building.

The village contains the "Priest's House", a late fifteenth-century building restored in 1867 and now owned by the National Trust; it contains a small museum about the area.
The commander of HMS Lutine, Captain Lancelot Skynner, came from Easton, where his father John was the rector for many years. Plaques on the former rectory (now Glebe House but known for a time as Lutine House) and in the church commemorate this and Captain Skynner. The frigate Lutine sank during a storm  in the West Frisian Islands on 9 October 1799, whilst carrying a large shipment of gold. Lloyd's of London has preserved her salvaged bell - the Lutine Bell - which is used for ceremonial purposes at their headquarters in London.
The head office of the Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply (CIPS) is located at Easton House in the village, close to the church.
Easton on the Hill Rural District existed from 1894 to 1935. The parish has its own parish council and was represented on East Northamptonshire Council and on the county council as part of the Prebendal electoral division. Easton on the Hill is represented in the House of Commons by the Member of Parliament for Corby. At the time of the 2001 census, the parish's population was 956 people.

The '''Guildhall of St George''' is a [[Grade I listed]] building in [[King's Lynn]], [[Norfolk]], England. The [[Guild]] of [[St George]] was founded in 1376 and constructed the Guildhall between 1410 and 1420. It is the largest extant [[guildhall]] in England. It has been in use as a [[theatre]] since 1445, making it the oldest theatre still operating in the [[United Kingdom]], and the only one still in existence in which [[William Shakespeare]] is believed to have performed. The building is in the ownership of the [[National Trust]], which has leased it to [[King's Lynn and West Norfolk]] borough council for hire as a music, performances, lectures and entertainment venue.

== History ==
=== Foundation ===
The guildhall was created for the Guild of St George at the beginning of the 15th century.{{sfn|Smith|1870|p=74}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shakespeare's Guildhall Trust {{!}} St George's {{!}} Kings Lynn, Norfolk |url=https://www.shakespearesguildhalltrust.org.uk/ |access-date=2021-01-28 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/norfolk/st-georges-guildhall/the-history-of-st-georges-guildhall|title=The history of St George's Guildhall|publisher=[[National Trust]]|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref> In 1406 the Guild of St George, founded in 1376, acquired re-claimed land on the bank of the [[River Great Ouse]] to build its hall. Constructed between 1410 and 1420, the hall was in use by 1428. In about 1500 the structure was strengthened by the addition of [[buttress]]es along the north wall.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.heritage.norfolk.gov.uk/record-details?MNF5483-St-George%27s-Guildhall-King-Street&Index=5017&RecordCount=61672&SessionID=8fa40d94-97f9-4d57-add8-7c8363fba659  |title=St George's Guildhall, King Street|publisher=Norfolk Heritage Explorer|access-date=30 August 2024}}</ref>

Following the Dissolution of the Guilds in 1547 control of the guildhall passed to the Lynn Corporation which retained ownership until 1814. In the late 17th century the brick-vaulted wine cellar was made in the undercroft, and access to this was continued under the later warehouses towards the river. The hall continued to serve as a theatre and public hall, as well as a court house, a school, and as a [[munitions]] store during the [[English Civil War]].<ref name="auto"/>

=== England's oldest theatre: 1445–1814===
The earliest record of a theatrical production is of a nativity play before a Guild feast in January 1445 featuring William, the barber in Grassmarket, and Richard Comber. The Guild regularly staged theatricals, including a procession on St George's Day which took place until 1546. After the Dissolution it was used by [[playing company|companies of players]]; the [[Queen Elizabeth's Men|Queen's Players]] performed regularly between 1585 and 1595. Recent academic research by Professor Matthew Woodcock, at the University of East Anglia, has supported the local tradition that [[William Shakespeare]] played at the guildhall with the [[Pembroke's Men|Earl of Pembroke's Men]] in 1593 when London theatres were closed by the plague. It is the only theatre left in England where Shakespeare is believed to have performed.{{efn|There is considerable evidence to support the claim that Shakespeare performed at St George's Guildhall but it is not definitive.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://westnorfolkartists.org/artscentre/pdfs/The_Case_for_Placing_Shakespeare_in_KL.pdf|first=Matthew|last=Woodcock|title=The Case for Placing Shakespeare in King's Lynn|publisher=[[University of East Anglia]]|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>}}<ref name="auto"/> Shakespeare's leading comic actor, [[Robert Armin]], was born in King's Lynn in 1565, the family living in what is now 78 High Street.  Armin was the first [[Feste]] in ''[[Twelfth Night]]'', Autolycus in ''[[A Winter's Tale]]'' and the Fool in ''[[King Lear]]'', and is credited with being a major influence on Shakespeare.<ref name="auto"/>

In the 17th century players continued to use the guildhall until the prohibition on plays imposed during the [[Commonwealth of England|Commonwealth]].  Theatricals resumed after the Restoration in 1660. The success of the playhouse led to the construction of the Theatre Royal in the town in 1813, and in 1814 the guildhall was sold. It was resold in 1826 to the Everards, a family of merchants who converted it into a warehouse.<ref name="auto"/>

===20th and 21st centuries===
In 1920 the Everard family sold the hall for £2,650 to G.M. Bridges and Son Ltd., theatrical set designers. Successful in the Victorian and Edwardian eras, and gaining [[Royal warrant of appointment (United Kingdom)|Royal warrant]]s for their work at [[Sandringham House]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kingslynncivicsociety.co.uk/heritage/the-guildhall-of-st-george/|title=The Guildhall of St. George|publisher=King's Lynn Civic Society|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref> the business declined with the advent of cinema. By 1946 the guildhall was derelict and scheduled for demolition. It was purchased by Alexander Penrose, son of [[J. Doyle Penrose]], who converted it to an arts centre. The building was restored 1948–51 by [[Marshall Sisson]] and vested in the National Trust. In 1951 the St George's Arts Trust took a long lease.<ref name="auto"/> The centre was opened by [[Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother]], for the first King's Lynn Festival on 24 July of that year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.edp24.co.uk/news/23834797.kings-lynn-shakespeares-stage-found-ancient-guildhall/|title=Shakespeare's stage found in ancient guildhall|publisher=[[Eastern Daily Press]]|date=5 October 2023|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>

Warehouses which form the building's courtyard were converted to galleries in 1963 by [[Ruth Roche, Baroness Fermoy|Lady Fermoy]] (lady-in-waiting to the Queen Mother) in memory of her husband, [[Maurice Roche, 4th Baron Fermoy|Lord Fermoy]], who had served as mayor of King's Lynn and as its member of parliament. In 1993 the [[King's Lynn and West Norfolk|Borough Council]] took over the lease.  Between 2011 and 2016 King's Lynn Arts Centre Trust managed the galleries. In 2019 the National Trust, King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council and the newly formed Shakespeare's Guildhall Trust formed a group to undertake redevelopment of the site. Although the Guildhall Trust was subsequently wound up, the remaining members of the group continued with planning.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.west-norfolk.gov.uk/downloads/download/396/st_georges_guildhall_complex|title=St Georges Guildhall Complex|publisher=King's Lynn & West Norfolk borough council|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>
{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=right|quote=Everyone interested in Shakespeare and in the theatres of his time must feel a thrill of excitement at the discovery of the only surviving boards on which he is likely to have performed|source=—Sir [[Stanley Wells]], President of the [[Shakespeare Birthplace Trust]], on the discovery of the [[medieval]] stage.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.west-norfolk.gov.uk/news/article/1512/theatre_discovers_medieval_stage_where_shakespeare_is_said_to_have_performed|title=Theatre discovers Medieval stage where Shakespeare is said to have performed|publisher=Kings Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council|date=5 October 2023|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>}}
In 2019 the guildhall was declared the priority project of the Town Deal for King's Lynn<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.west-norfolk.gov.uk/info/20010/regeneration/837/kings_lynn_town_deal | title=King's Lynn Town Deal|publisher=King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref> and a development plan for the area was finalised.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.west-norfolk.gov.uk/news/article/1419/guildhall_design_team_announced|title=Guildhall design team announced|publisher=Kings Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.visionkingslynn.co.uk/projects/st-georges-guildhall-and-creative-hub/#documents | title=St George's Guildhall and Creative Hub|publisher=Kings Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref> On 5 January each year, the theatre commemorates the anniversary of the first recorded performance there in 1445.<ref>{{Cite web|date=7 January 2020|title=Anniversary at King's Lynn's medieval gem|url=https://www.lynnnews.co.uk/whats-on/anniversary-at-kings-lynns-medieval-gem-9095606/|access-date=28 January 2021|publisher=Lynn News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.discoverkingslynn.com/news/578th-anniversary-of-the-first-guildhall-performance-to-be-marked-with-a-new-artwork/|title=578th Anniversary of the first Guildhall performance to be marked with a new artwork|publisher=discover King's Lynn|date=22 December 2022|access-date=20 November 2023}}</ref>  In 2022 [[Tim FitzHigham]] was made Creative Director for the site.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.thestage.co.uk/news/appointments/comedian-tim-fitzhigham-to-lead-revival-of-st-georges-guildhall-in-kings-lynn | title=Comedian Tim FitzHigham to lead revival of St George's Guildhall in King's Lynn|publisher=[[The Stage]]|access-date=6 October 2023 }}</ref> In 2023 the council appointed [[Haworth Tompkins]], an architectural practice with experience in the redevelopment of historic theatres, to lead a redevelopment of the guildhall to create a cultural centre with a Shakespearean theatre as its centrepiece.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.west-norfolk.gov.uk/news/article/1419/guildhall_design_team_announced|title=Guildhall design team announced|publisher=King's Lynn and West Norfolk Borough Council|date=24 May 2023|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bdonline.co.uk/news/haworth-tompkins-wins-job-to-restore-britains-oldest-working-theatre/5123359.article|title=Haworth Tompkins wins job to restore Britain's oldest working theatre|first=Tom|last=Lowe|publisher=[[Haworth Tompkins]]|date=24 May 2023|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref> Work is due for completion in 2026.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/competitions/st-georges-guildhall-phase-2-7-kings-lynn|title=St George's Guildhall Phase 2-7, King's Lynn|first=Merlin|last=Fulcher|publisher=[[Architects' Journal]]|date=3 January 2023|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>

During renovations in 2023, a wooden floor was uncovered which the theatre considers was likely the flooring in place when Shakespeare performed there in 1592–93. [[Dendrochronology|Tree-ring dating]] and a survey of how the building was assembled date the floor boards to between 1417 and 1430. It survived under a later floor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-67007980|first=Colin|last=Paterson|title=Stage that once hosted William Shakespeare found, claims Norfolk theatre|publisher=[[BBC News]]|date=5 October 2023|access-date=5 October 2023}}</ref> In August 2024, a 600-year-old doorway, thought to be the entrance to a dressing room once used by Shakespeare, was discovered when two noticeboards and layers of plasterboard were removed from a wall on the ground floor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gordon-Farleigh |first=Neve |date=2024-08-21 |title=Theatre makes 'mind boggling' Shakespeare discovery |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1d7xe25xe2o |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=[[BBC News]] |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Architecture and description ==
The Guildhall of [[St George]] is the largest surviving medieval guildhall in the country. It is a Grade I listed building.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1290960|desc=Guildhall of St George, King's Lynn and West Norfolk|grade=I|access-date=5 October 2023}}</ref> Built of brick, and of two storeys with a [[gable roof]], its dimensions are  32.6 x 8.8 m (107 x 29 feet).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.shakespearesguildhalltrust.org.uk/|title=Shakespeare's Guildhall Trust|access-date=5 October 2023}}</ref> The building occupies a long, narrow site which was once a [[burgage]] plot between King Street and the river. The theatre stands on the raised upper floor, above an [[undercroft]]. The roof is to a [[hammerbeam roof|hammerbeam]] design.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://database.theatrestrust.org.uk/resources/theatres/show/2164-guildhall-of-st-george|title=Guildhall of St George|publisher=Theatres Trust|access-date=6 October 2023}}</ref>
